subtasks.name: Review incoming applications
subtasks.description: Recruiters read the several hundred applications received for each warehouse and driver posting to understand who has applied.
subtasks.rationale: Reading and sorting applications is routine and high in volume. Errors here are caught when candidates are shortlisted.

subtasks.name: Shortlist candidates by hand
subtasks.description: Recruiters currently pick which applicants move forward by hand, weighing experience and fit for the posting.
subtasks.rationale: Shortlisting shapes who gets a job chance. It relies on recruiter experience, and people could reasonably disagree.

subtasks.name: Rank applicants with ML tool
subtasks.description: A vendor's machine-learning tool would score and rank applicants for each posting so that the best-fitting ones rise to the top.
subtasks.rationale: The ranking directly drives who is considered for hiring. Errors or bias would change outcomes for many applicants.

subtasks.name: Reject applicants below cut-off
subtasks.description: The tool would automatically reject applicants whose score falls below a set cut-off, with no person reviewing the result.
subtasks.rationale: An automatic rejection is a hiring decision affecting livelihood. The cut-off rule is simple but its effects are significant.

subtasks.name: Spot disengagement in one-to-ones
subtasks.description: Team leads currently try to notice signs of disengagement in staff through their regular one-to-one conversations.
subtasks.rationale: Reading people draws on experience and is hard to write down. Informal observation alone does not decide anything formally.

subtasks.name: Score employee sentiment from chat
subtasks.description: The tool would continuously analyze workplace chat messages and give each employee a sentiment score.
subtasks.rationale: Scores about identifiable staff feed HR follow-up. Errors could harm trust and employment standing, and the monitoring runs constantly.

subtasks.name: Flag low performers and disengaged staff
subtasks.description: HR uses the sentiment scores to flag employees seen as low performers or disengaged and to select them for follow-up.
subtasks.rationale: Flagging shapes how managers treat employees and may lead to performance management. A wrong flag can hurt livelihood and trust.

assumptions: The tool scores applicants using the content of their applications.
Rejected applicants are not reviewed by a person before being told.
Sentiment scores are linked to named employees, not only to teams.
HR relies on the scores when choosing whom to follow up with.
Employees may not be fully aware their chat messages are analyzed.
clarifyingQuestions: Does anyone review applicants rejected below the cut-off before they are notified?
Are sentiment scores shown for individual employees or only for teams?
What does follow-up involve for a flagged employee, and could it affect their performance record?

narrative.executiveSummary: The verdict is Redesign, with an AIA-inspired indicative tier of IV, because the case scores applicants and employee sentiment, which bears on decisions about people. The OIPC BC guidance under BC PIPA is a blocker: the regulator expects ongoing sentiment scoring to be replaced by a narrow, overt, time-limited measure, and the privacy officer, with HR and the product owner, is the likely owner. BC PIPA and the BC Human Rights Code likely apply, so the team should consider notice, proportionality and bias testing before a pilot.
narrative.splitNarrative: AI does it (spot-checked) for Review incoming applications. AI drafts, a person checks and signs off for Spot disengagement in one-to-ones. A person does it (AI may assist) for Shortlist candidates by hand, Rank applicants with ML tool, Reject applicants below cut-off, Score employee sentiment from chat, and Flag low performers and disengaged staff. This is a starting split that the team will move as evidence comes in. The next split review is 2027-02-26, then quarterly.
leverNarratives: Let the team that does the work decide which steps the AI does and change that over time, using tools and labels shared with other teams. Keep the guardrail Shared platform in place: common tools, common labels and visible splits. The direct cost is some automation efficiency, since you give up part of the consistency and scale of one split shared by all teams.

Let the team adjust the split as it learns, on top of a fixed base of data formats, hand-off points and escalation thresholds, and re-check it quarterly. Keep the guardrail Standardized base in place: agreed data formats, handoff points and escalation thresholds. The direct cost is some automation efficiency, because the team spends attention adjusting and outputs vary more above the base.

Hold regular joint working sessions with the vendor's delivery team, with an internal AI steward who owns the correction channel. Keep the guardrail Retained differentiation in place: dedicated time for technical and for domain work. The direct cost is some standalone depth on each side, as experts and AI specialists spend time on each other's work.
narrative.rolloutNarrative: Days 1–30, Foundation & guardrails: redesign the scoring, clear every blocker, assign owners, set up the shared platform and standardized base, and measure baselines. Days 31–60, Shadow pilot & calibration: run the AI in shadow mode, calibrate thresholds, feed corrections back, and keep people on consequential steps. Days 61–90, Controlled scale & audit: go live in controlled increments, hold the first split review and audit a sample of decisions. KPIs to track: Time to shortlist; Decision quality on non-routine cases (sampled expert review); Corrections fed back into the system per month.
